question: Why do first-time investors start SIPs, and what do they expect?
headline: People rarely say why they started, but when they say what they expected, it is a fixed-return product.
answer: Only 41 of 899 items state a reason for starting (mostly tax saving and a specific goal), so the 'why' is a gap for interviews. Expectations are clearer: when stated, they describe a guaranteed or calculator-like outcome ('a guaranteed minimum', 'a known amount after 2-3 years', '15% for 20 years', 'returns higher than an FD'). Many believe a SIP is a product with a validity, term or payout, which is why 'Misunderstands how a SIP works' is the most common theme overall (170 mentions, 39% from first-timers). YouTube is the most-named influence (33 items).
confidence: Medium for expectations, low for start reasons (sparse).
quick: Only 41 of 899 posts say why they started (mostly tax saving or a goal), so the reason is a gap for interviews.
When stated, expectations sound fixed: "a guaranteed minimum", "returns higher than an FD".

quick_conf: Medium for expectations, low for start reasons.

question: How does behaviour change after starting?
headline: After a bad experience, people don't just stop: they switch to manual payments, stop looking, time the market or move platforms.
answer: 131 items describe a change in behaviour. The patterns: moving from autopay to paying by hand after failed or cancelled debits; deleting the app or not checking so the SIP survives ('na rahega na dikhega'); replacing the SIP with lump sums on dips; opening many SIPs at once and then consolidating into a few; cutting the SIP to repay a loan faster; deleting a SIP to restart it with a step-up; moving SIPs to another platform. Continuers who change behaviour mostly raise the amount as income grows.
confidence: Medium: patterns repeat across sources, counts are small per pattern.
quick: 131 posts describe a change in behaviour after starting.
Common shifts: autopay to manual payments, not opening the app, lump sums on dips, moving platforms.
Continuers who change mostly raise the amount as income grows.
quick_conf: Medium: patterns repeat, but each one is small.

question: What drives people to pause, reduce or stop?
headline: Most drop-offs are the system or the investor's understanding failing, not money running out. Market falls are the trigger far more often than the cause.
answer: Of 338 items showing a drop signal, 145 trace to operations (autopay and mandate failures, app glitches, fund-side suspensions, pause and change friction, no support) and 151 to understanding (returns below expectations, anxiety at red numbers, misconceptions). 32 are money or life pressures, mostly Reddit posts weighing a SIP against a loan or a big expense, and 8 are moves to another product or platform. Of the 124 posts that say how a SIP ended, 72 ended without the investor choosing to stop: the fund or platform cancelled it (36), a payment failed or lapsed (29), or a pause was never resumed (7). Among the 76 who say they actually stopped, the largest single cause is a fund or platform cancelling the SIP (19). Market falls appear as a trigger in 99 items, yet 54 of those people are still continuing; what tips people over is what they expected or what they saw, not the fall itself.
confidence: High for the ops-vs-understanding split; source mix shapes it (see Sources).
quick: 338 drop signals: 145 trace to operations, 151 to understanding, only 32 to money pressure.
72 of 124 SIPs that ended weren't ended by choice: cancelled by fund or platform (36), payment failed (29), pause never resumed (7).
Market falls appear in 99 posts, yet 54 of those people still invest.

question: What do they check, and how often?
headline: They watch the returns number, and early red numbers are the moment of greatest risk.
answer: Few say how often they check (12 items; 7 say daily), so frequency is a gap. What they look at is clear: the portfolio returns screen (128 items), daily gain or loss, XIRR versus absolute return, NAV. 'Is this normal?' questions about flat or negative early returns form a recurring need (22 items) with one of the highest drop links of any need (73%). Some cope by not looking at all.
confidence: Medium for what they check, low for frequency.
quick: They watch the returns screen (128 posts): daily gain or loss, XIRR, NAV.
"Is this normal?" about early red returns comes up 22 times and 73% of those posts show a drop signal.
How often they check is rarely stated (12 posts), so it is a gap.
quick_conf: Medium for what they check, low for how often.

question: What confuses them inside the app?
headline: Confusion concentrates on SIP management: what stop, pause, delete and cancel actually do.
answer: Of 334 confused items, 127 are about SIP management, 41 about autopay and mandates, 32 about fund pages. Recurring confusions: whether stopping or deleting a SIP loses the money already invested, when a cancellation takes effect, why a SIP shows paused or 'modification in progress', why a step-up or amount change makes the fund house send a 'SIP cancelled' email while the app still shows it active, platform versus AMC-registered SIPs, and direct versus regular plans. Some of these lead to accidental cancellations.
quick: Of 334 confused posts, 127 are about managing the SIP, 41 about autopay, 32 about fund pages.
Top questions: does stopping lose my money, when does a cancellation apply, why does it say paused or "modification in progress".
Some of these confusions end in accidental cancellations.

question: What do they do outside the app to understand, compare or validate decisions?
headline: They ask strangers in YouTube comments and forums the questions the app could answer.
answer: 138 YouTube comments ask creators directly about their own SIP, mostly mechanics (40) and fear of losses (20). Forum and Reddit threads (460 relevant items) are dominated by misconceptions (64), pause and skip mechanics (57), mandate failures (48) and fund-side suspensions (46). Reddit posts also show people asking strangers to sanity-check a first portfolio before they start. A few use a second app to track returns or verify balances.
confidence: High that this behaviour exists; the sample over-represents people who ask in public.

Forums and Reddit (460 posts) focus on misconceptions, pause rules, mandate failures and fund suspensions.
Some ask strangers to check a first portfolio before they start.
quick_conf: High that this happens; people who ask in public are over-represented.

question: How do continuers differ from drop-offs?
headline: Continuers understand averaging, automate and use flexibility; drop-offs hit broken operations and broken expectations.
answer: Among 258 continuers, 26% show understanding of long-term investing or averaging, 7% credit automation and 4% a trusted reassurance source; almost none of the 338 drop-off items do (no more than 4 of 338). Continuers also use pause, skip and step-up more (19% vs 13%). Drop-offs over-index on app trust problems (18% vs 4%), returns below expectations (12% vs 2%), no help when stuck (11% vs 0%), money pressure (11% vs 2%) and fund suspensions (10% vs 3%).
confidence: Medium-high: same-source comparison, but continuers who never post are missing.

question: Do patterns differ by income stability, age, source of money or influencer?
headline: Mostly unanswerable from public text; journey stage and first-timer status are the only usable cuts.
answer: Income, age and money source are unstated in at least 94% of items, so comparisons would be noise; this is a target for interviews, not a finding. What the data supports: first-timers (237 items) show a drop signal less often in what they post (24% vs 43%), but when they do it is mainly anxiety at losses (16 of 56), misconceptions and unmet expectations, while experienced investors drop because of operations and money pressure. The few irregular-income items describe a fixed monthly amount that doesn't fit how money arrives.
confidence: Low for income, age and influencer; medium for first-timer vs experienced.
quick: Income, age and money source are unstated in at least 94% of posts: a question for interviews, not a finding.
First-timers post a drop signal less often (24% vs 43%); when they do, it is mainly anxiety at losses and misconceptions.
Experienced investors drop mostly over operations and money pressure.
quick_conf: Low for income and age; medium for first-timer vs experienced.

question: What unmet needs come up again and again?
headline: Flex instead of stop, know what stopping does, a guided start, and payments that just work.
answer: 401 items state an unmet need, grouped into 15 recurring needs. The largest: flex the SIP instead of stopping it (66), know what stopping, pausing or missing really does to my money (65), a guided start for first-timers (52), payments that work with a clear way back after a failure (46). The needs most tied to drop-off: being told why a SIP was stopped by the fund or platform (81%) and knowing whether early returns are normal (73%).
confidence: High for the top four; groups were formed by Claude and counted by code.
